reason: The hypothesis relies on the catalytic benefits of Pt on high-entropy supports (E1, E2) and the CO-poisoning resistance of single-atom Pt in high-entropy alloys (E3). However, E1 and E2 describe Pt nanoparticles, not atomically dispersed Pt, and E3 addresses methanol oxidation, not automotive exhaust conditions with H2O and NO. The cited evidence therefore does not directly support the key premise that atomically dispersed Pt in a multi-principal-element alloy will provide enhanced low-temperature oxidation, poisoning resistance, and durability under the specified automotive exhaust conditions
premises: Pt nanoparticles on high-entropy oxide (HEO) support enable low-temperature CO oxidation and exhibit thermal stability after aging up to 800 °C.
Atomic-level dispersion and electron transfer between HEO and Pt nanoparticles prevent Pt over-oxidation/reduction, boosting durability.
Isolating Pt atoms in a material can avoid CO poisoning.
High-entropy alloyed single-atom Pt sites resist CO poisoning and maintain high activity due to synergistic removal of adsorbed CO by surrounding elements.
